AI has transformed software engineering. It's changing nearly every knowledge-based profession.

 - Why sales is the next profession to be transformed by AI
 - How AI is changing software development and product velocity
 - Why sales reps need to become revenue AI consultants

items.title: "Zero Chance" AI Bubble Doesn't Pop (Here's Who's Safe) | Geoffrey Moore, Author & Venture Partner
items.author: Sam Jacobs, AJ Bruno & Asad Zaman
items.summary:
Geoffrey Moore, author of Crossing the Chasm (over 1 million copies sold) and Zone to Win, and an advisor to the CEOs of Microsoft, Salesforce, and Cisco, joins Sam Jacobs, AJ Bruno, and Asad Zaman for a first appearance on Topline. Topics include whether agentic AI has crossed the chasm, why there's "zero chance" the AI bubble doesn't pop (and who will make it out the other side!), how startups win in a downturn, and how the Zone to Win framework is useful to help move AI pilots out of incubation and into the core business. Plus, a closer look at the SaaS-pocalypse and Salesforce's platform play, trapped value as the only durable moat, the hierarchy of powers behind today's valuations, whether AI has to eat the labor budget to pay off, and whether Geoffrey would buy the Anthropic IPO at a $2 trillion valuation.
 Key Takeaways:
 - The AI bubble will pop, but the category leaders will be fine. "There is zero chance that this bubble doesn't pop. We're so far over our skis in terms of valuations, it's crazy," said Geoffrey, pointing to circular financing that echoes the dot-com era. The survivors are the number 1 and number 2 players: "The winners are actually gonna win… But 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10? No."
 - Most AI initiatives are stuck in the incubation zone. "People were piloting like crazy and having great success" said of the last two years of enterprise AI pilots... but then they got stuck. The Zone to Win fix is to make the productivity zone customer zero, re-engineering internal shared services first, then bring the new technology to the sales team use case by use case rather than all at once.
 - Where are moats today? Geoffrey points to trapped value as one type of moat. Trapped value analysis is a method to continually discover the new ways you can be irreplaceable to your customers, and stay ahead of the market.
 - The ROI from AI won't come mainly from cutting headcount. "I think they're coming from quality improvement and latency reduction, not from labor reduction," said Geoffrey. For the next decade, probabilistic agents will sit in front of deterministic systems of record with a human checking in between, because "AI can be accountable, but it cannot be responsible."

items.title: The Man Who Led 100+ CROs (Even OpenAI's) | John McMahon - 5x Post-IPO CRO / The GOAT
items.author: Sam Jacobs, AJ Bruno & Asad Zaman
items.summary:
John McMahon, a five-time public company CRO whose team at PTC created MEDDIC, joins Sam Jacobs, AJ Bruno, and Asad Zaman on building enterprise sales teams that last. Topics include the PTC lineage that has produced over 100 CROs, including OpenAI's Dali Rajic, why he hires on characteristics over resumes, whether a CRO who never carried a bag can lead, and how first-time CROs should work with their CEO. Plus, capped commissions at Anthropic, why AI makes lazy reps lazier, what conversational intelligence tools miss in deal qualification, and quick takes on Dali, Carlos at Harness, Dev Ittycheria, and Chris at Cognition.
 Key Takeaways:
 - Hire on characteristics, not resumes. John sorts candidates by skills, knowledge, experience and characteristics, and the last one is the hardest to teach: "I've always hired on characteristics. So I'll take someone with less experience but great characteristics." He looks for intelligence, drive, coachability, adaptability and integrity, because when a hire fails, "it's always a character flaw."
 - Don't take the CRO seat before you're ready. John once refused a promotion Dali pushed him for: "I told him, I'm not gonna do that to you because you're not ready… you're gonna fail. Your ego's not gonna be able to take it." For John, readiness comes down to whether you can recruit, coach, and lead people who actually want to follow you.
 - Talk to the CEO as a partner. Plenty of first-time CROs hold the C-level title without acting like the CEO's peer, and John coaches them to speak up: "You're the CRO. You have a fiduciary responsibility. Tell the CEO specifically what you think is wrong with the business." Blaming revenue problems on the product "is a non-starter," so come with a solution and talk like a business owner.
 - AI hasn't changed the methodology. John sees AI mostly as a research tool, and "it makes the really good sales reps better, and it makes the lazy sales reps lazier." He is just as blunt about conversational intelligence: "All they're doing is verifying that something was said, but there's no true qualification." Qualifying still means knowing whether you're talking to a champion, a coach, or the enemy.

items.title: $682M Public CEO: "The Magic of 80% Gross Margin" | CEO @ Yext, Michael Walrath
items.author: Sam Jacobs, AJ Bruno & Asad Zaman
items.summary:
Michael Walrath, CEO of Yext, is back on Topline to explain how Yext went from breakeven to 31% EBITDA margins on an 80% gross margin business, after halving its headcount and using its balance sheet to buy back roughly 35% of every share it ever issued. He joins Sam Jacobs, AJ Bruno, and Asad Zaman to argue that the old rules of business still apply: why VC math and founder math are different games, why employees lose the most when an overvalued startup like Airtable lands far below its peak valuation, and why this market feels like 2004. Plus, why Yext stopped doing earnings calls and replaced most stock comp with cash, why cutting the bottom half of a sales team can raise bookings, and how Yext is blurring the lines between AEs, account managers, CSMs and sales engineers.
 Key Takeaways:
 - Real profitability turns any growth into fuel. As Michael put it, "when you're actually profitable, like really profitable, then any growth becomes hugely accretive." With 80% gross margins and 31% EBITDA margins, "Every incremental dollar, I can spend 45 cents of it and not affect my margins in any way," so a left-for-dead software company can fund its own growth whatever the market says it's worth.
 - Chase growth only where it actually exists. "Nothing's more powerful than growth at creating value. Nothing is more destructive to value than chasing growth when the growth isn't there," said Michael. Airtable avoided the trap by leaving its cash on the balance sheet, while Yext once spent 74% of revenue on sales and marketing into a declining growth rate.
 - Cutting your weakest sellers can grow bookings. When 20% of reps make quota and the bottom half brings in 20% of bookings, the spreadsheet says cutting them costs you that 20%. "It's not even close to true. It's the opposite," said Michael (his numbers were illustrative). Yext now has fewer, better sellers, and is "effectively eliminating all distinction between go-to-market roles" in favor of teams that own books of customers.
 - Stock comp can turn your own employees into sellers of your stock. Most people sold their RSUs the day they vested, and every quarterly issuance meant the company sold shares to cover taxes too. "The last thing you need are more sellers of your stock every quarter," said Michael, so Yext now pays most employees more cash and points long-term believers to its employee stock purchase plan.

items.title: AI Revenue Is Real. But Will It Last? | Amy Konary, Founder & Chair, Subscribed Institute @ Zuora
items.author: Sam Jacobs, AJ Bruno & Asad Zaman
items.summary:
Amy Konary, Founder & Chair of The Subscribed Institute at Zuora, coined the term SaaS as an IDC analyst around 2000, when her first forecast sized the whole market at $40 million. She joins Sam Jacobs, AJ Bruno, and Asad Zaman for the first in-person Topline to ask whether AI company economics are a house of cards, and whether circular financing and double counting are real problems. Plus, why POCs have stopped being a pipeline signal, experimental revenue versus true ARR, a new leverage index for sticky revenue, tokens versus credits, and how close outcome pricing can really get.
 Key Takeaways:
 - Treat POCs as a weak pipeline signal. As Amy put it, "it used to be that hands-on product was a really good signal from a pipeline perspective, but everyone's doing POCs just to kick the tires, but actually has no mandate to buy." Many are free, production-ready builds, and very few convert.
 - Usage alone won't tell you which revenue will last. Amy scores customers on scope and workflows, trust in the system's outputs, and how much of their own context they upload, because "you can have 2 customers with the exact same usage, but very different leverage." Low leverage means "That revenue is less durable."
 - Pure usage pricing can leave you as exposed as seats did. "If you're just tracking usage, and usage is highly experimental, and usage decreases over time as people optimize the tools, you're in the same vulnerable position you were in with seats," said Amy, who expects hybrid models with a smaller, trackable outcome piece.
 - Build for durability without rigidity. "So I think there's a difference between durability and rigidity," Amy said, and her metaphor is bamboo: one of the strongest construction materials, yet flexible, anchored by a clear focus on the customer's progress.

items.title: Turning AI Tokens Into ROI (That You Can Measure) | CEO @ Paid, Manny Medina
items.author: Sam Jacobs, AJ Bruno & Asad Zaman
items.summary:
Manny Medina, Co-Founder and CEO of Paid, the monetization platform for AI agents, and the founder who took Outreach from nothing, joins Sam Jacobs, AJ Bruno, and Asad Zaman in person on how to price AI agents once seats stop making sense. Topics include why every SaaS company needs its own agents before someone else's run on its MCP layer, why a token is the wrong unit of value, and the itemized phone bill every agent builder owes its buyers. Plus, why fixed-price deals win logos but stall expansion, the case for 40% to 60% gross margins in the agent era, and what Satya Nadella told Manny in a green room.
  Key Takeaways:
  - Price the work your agent does, not the seats it fills. In SaaS you sell 100 seats, procurement sees 20 in heavy use, and the renewal shrinks to 50. With agents, "if you've sold 100 seats and only 2 were hyper-users, you don't care because you're charging for all the uses and all the value those 2 seats were getting." For now that pricing lives between effort and output, because true outcome pricing needs attribution, and as Manny put it, "Attribution is really hard."
  - Make the bill readable before you argue about ROI. Manny compares it to the old itemized phone bill, where you went straight to the biggest line and asked, "Did I really call Pakistan from New York?" Tokens can't play that role: "A token should not be a unit of value for charging because a token is really kind of like the inside secret." Show the buyer the research, deck, or analysis the agent produced, because "explainability is like the first rung in the ladder."
  - Fixed pricing is easy money that boxes you in at renewal. Enterprises are buying one of each right now, so "new logo is not hard. Expansion is hard." Teams that land logos on fixed price hit the first renewal with nowhere to go, which is why Paid opens with a monetization consultant and takes a percentage of revenue: "You grow, I grow." - Plan for thinner margins and narrower markets. Manny learned Amazon's margins cold (books 20%, electronics 7%, jewelry 3%) and calls SaaS's 70 to 80% an anomaly of cheap money: "I feel like a normal, you know, software business will be running on 40% margins, 60% tops."

items.author: Sam Jacobs, AJ Bruno & Asad Zaman

Harvey's gross margin fell from roughly positive 50% at the start of 2026 to negative 50% by June, so every $1 of revenue cost $1.50 to deliver. Sam Jacobs, CEO of Pavilion, AJ Bruno, CEO of QuotaPath, and Asad Zaman, CEO of STA, go hosts-only on when AI growth justifies margins like that, why open weight models are no substitute for frontier intelligence, and what happens to the application layer if the exuberant market funding it goes away. Plus, AJ's 100x raise from 2021, a 68% jump in tech M&A and what it means for employee equity, and a Bulls and Bears round on AI catastrophe before 2031.
 Key Takeaways:
 - Negative gross margins can be a phase if there's a way out. Sam's straw man: "Above 200% growth, I can tolerate bad margins temporarily if you can show me you have a path to a good business." Between 100% and 200% he wants "a clear improving trajectory," and below 50% the margins have to be good.
 - Cheaper models fix the margin line but can break the product. Asad likened the switch to open weight models to "going from hiring people only from Harvard to then going and hiring people from the worst university you can find or some mid-tier university and saying it's the same thing." That leaves application companies "completely at the behest of these model companies."
 - The 2021 hangover is still on cap tables. AJ raised QuotaPath's Series B "at a 100x valuation in '21," but with SaaS multiples at "1x or less than 1x," he said, "If I wanted to go sell QuotaPath today, I really couldn't find a buyer." items.title: The Operator's Roadmap for AI in 2026 - Lily Luo
items.author: Justin Norris
items.summary:
Justin and Lily reflect on their parallel journeys diving deep into AI throughout 2025. They discuss why most AI content misses the mark for operators and system builders working within corporate constraints, share lessons from building production AI tools, and explore what's next for bringing these capabilities into the enterprise.
Guest: Lily Luo — Systems & Operations Leader, Author of Applied AI for MOps Substack
Read more of Justin's thoughts on AI Builders: The operator's roadmap for AI in 2026
KEY TOPICS
The Gap in AI Content Most resources target researchers or GTM engineers focused on outbound automation. There's little guidance for operators dealing with cloud tools, security, and corporate complexity. That creates an opportunity to define best practices for this underserved audience.
2025 Project Highlights Lily built an "Analysis Dossier" tool that generates full account research reports at the click of a button. Justin replaced a vendor intelligence tool with a custom system using Retool and a conversational agent.
Lessons Learned Start with tightly scoped AI steps in linear workflows for reliability. Pre-process insights asynchronously rather than relying on real-time agent calculations. Match tools to use cases. Failures teach more than successes.
Atlas: Lily's Autonomous Agent Runs on Google Cloud and wakes every 4 hours to research and progress projects. Uses a three-layer memory architecture: identity, temporal journal, and knowledge graph. Can push its own code and interact with other agents.
2026 Outlook Focus on scalability, reduced hallucination, and team enablement. Build infrastructure that unlocks flexible, ad-hoc use cases. Bridge the gap between AI capabilities and enterprise readiness.
The Human Side Working closely with AI changes how you think. Boundaries matter—don't let AI become a crutch.
RESOURCES

Applied AI for MOps — Lily's Substack
AI Builders Blog — Justin's Substack
Tools mentioned: Claude Code, Gemini, ChatGPT, Zapier, Retool, Dust, Azure AI Foundry, Letta, VS Code

ONE TIP FOR GETTING STARTED
Pick a real pain point. Start with low-code tools you already know. Test relentlessly. Expect to fail—and learn from it.
